title: Nebuchadnezzar’s Decree
voicePrompt: In your own words, explain how this chapter traces Nebuchadnezzar's journey from pride to humility — the dream of the tree, God's judgment, and the king's final acknowledgment that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.

questions.stem: According to the chapter, what makes Nebuchadnezzar's decree a striking example for us to follow?
options: He boasted of his conquests to all people, nations, and languages
He was willing to publicly tell what God had done for him in the way of humiliation and chastisement, not just blessings
He commanded all nations to worship the God of Israel
He refused to acknowledge any fault on his own part
questions.explanation: The chapter says people are ready to tell what God has done in the way of benefits, but 'We ought to be no less ready to tell what God has done for us in the way of humiliation and chastisements; and Nebuchadnezzar sets us a good example in this respect.'

questions.stem: The chapter notes that God chose 'the most unlikely time' and 'the most unlikely means' to humble Nebuchadnezzar. What were they?
options: A military defeat at the height of a battle
A rebellion among his own counselors during a famine
A time when he was at rest and secure, troubled by means of a dream
A plague that struck Babylon while he traveled abroad
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that the most unlikely time — when he 'felt most at rest and secure' — was taken, and the most unlikely means — 'a dream' — was selected, since this warrior whom no foe could terrify 'was made a terror to himself.'

questions.stem: How does the chapter say the great tree symbolizes Nebuchadnezzar's reign?
options: It showed only external glory and splendor, with no internal worth
It represented a kingdom that oppressed and starved its subjects
It had both external glory and internal excellences, affording protection, support, and prosperity to all its subjects
It stood for the brevity and weakness of his short reign
questions.explanation: The chapter says the tree's 'external glory and splendor were great; but this was not all of it... It had internal excellences,' representing that Nebuchadnezzar 'ruled his kingdom in such a way as to afford the fullest protection, support, and prosperity to all his subjects.'

questions.stem: What lesson about mercy does the chapter draw from the command to leave the stump of the roots in the earth?
options: It shows that God's judgments are always purely destructive
It shows the mercy God mingles with his judgments, preserving a source of future growth — unlike the wicked who will finally be destroyed root and branch
It proves the tree would never be cut down at all
It teaches that Nebuchadnezzar's punishment was permanent
questions.explanation: The chapter titles this point 'The mercy that God mingles with his judgments,' noting the stump was left so 'the source of future growth and greatness might be left,' contrasting the wicked who 'shall be destroyed both root and branch' with no mercy mingled.

questions.stem: The chapter calls the phrase 'let seven times pass over him' an important key to prophetic interpretation. What rule does it establish?
options: A 'time' always means exactly one literal day
Since this is plain literal narration fulfilled over seven years (per Josephus), a 'time' denotes one year — and in symbolic prophecy a 'time' is 360 years
Seven times means seven thousand years in all prophecy
The number seven is purely symbolic and has no time value
questions.explanation: The chapter says this is 'plain, literal narration,' that Josephus reports Nebuchadnezzar was driven out for 'seven years,' so 'A "time," then, denotes one year.' In symbolic prophecy a 'time' is 'a prophetic year, or, each day standing for a year, three hundred and sixty literal years.'

questions.stem: Why did Daniel sit 'astonied for one hour' before interpreting the dream?
options: Because he could not understand the meaning of the dream
Because he feared the magicians would oppose him
Not from difficulty interpreting it, but because it was so delicate to announce such a terrible judgment to a king who had shown him nothing but favor
Because he doubted the dream came from God
questions.explanation: The chapter states Daniel's hesitation 'did not arise from any difficulty he had in interpreting the dream, but from its being so delicate a matter to make it known to the king,' since Daniel had received 'nothing but favor' from him.

questions.stem: What was the immediate trigger for the judgment finally falling on Nebuchadnezzar?
options: He executed Daniel for the unwelcome interpretation
While walking in the palace he boasted, 'Is not this great Babylon, that I have built... by the might of my power,' forgetting the source of his greatness
He set up another golden image to be worshipped
He invaded a neighboring kingdom against God's warning
questions.explanation: The chapter recounts that after twelve months of cherished pride, the king looked on Babylon and exclaimed, 'Is not this great Babylon, that I have built?' — at which 'a voice from heaven again announces the threatened judgment,' and his reason departed.

questions.stem: How does the chapter describe Nebuchadnezzar's condition after his reason returned at the end of seven years?
options: He relapsed into idolatry and was deposed by Evil-merodach
His first act was to bless the Most High; his honor and kingdom were restored, and he likely died in the faith of the God of Israel
He remained mad until his death and never recovered his throne
He renounced God entirely and was forgotten by his counselors
questions.explanation: The chapter says his 'first act then was to bless the Most High,' his 'honor and brightness returned,' he was 'once more established in the kingdom,' and 'it is probable that he did not again relapse into idolatry, but died in the faith of the God of Israel.'
